sections.title: QUESTION 1: Reading for Comprehension
sections.instructions: Read the text below, then answer the questions.

context.title: Practice passage: The Tyranny of the Five-Star Review (written for FreeSheet)
context.text:
[1] Last month I ate at a small restaurant in Bloemfontein that served the best lamb curry I have ever tasted. The owner, a cheerful woman called Mrs Pillay, asked me as I left whether I would 'please, please' leave a review. Not a good review, I noticed. A five-star review. Anything less, she explained, and her restaurant would sink beneath the hundreds of others on the app.

[2] We now live in a world where everything is rated: our taxi drivers, our plumbers, our dentists, even the people who deliver our groceries. On the surface this is democratic. Why should a restaurant critic's opinion matter more than mine? But the system has a cruel flaw. When every rating is expected to be perfect, four stars, which once meant 'very good', has come to mean 'something went wrong'.

[3] The result is a strange kind of dishonesty. We give five stars because we feel sorry for the driver, or because we are afraid of seeming mean. The ratings stop telling us anything at all. And the people being rated, who often depend on them for their income, live in constant fear of a single bad day.

[4] I gave Mrs Pillay five stars. She deserved them. But I wonder how many of her neighbours deserved four, and are now out of business.

questions.prompt: In which city is the restaurant in the passage?
Match each tone word to its meaning.
Comment on the structure of the passage, referring to its beginning and ending.
questions.memo:
✓ It is circular: it starts and ends with Mrs Pillay (1)
✓ The ending adds a thought-provoking twist about the neighbours who went out of business (1)

sections.title: QUESTION 4: Poetry: Tone, Imagery and Theme
sections.instructions: Read the text below, then answer the questions.

context.title: London – William Blake (1794; public domain)
context.text:
I wander thro' each charter'd street,
Near where the charter'd Thames does flow.
And mark in every face I meet
Marks of weakness, marks of woe.

In every cry of every Man,
In every Infants cry of fear,
In every voice: in every ban,
The mind-forg'd manacles I hear

How the Chimney-sweepers cry
Every blackning Church appalls,
And the hapless Soldiers sigh
Runs in blood down Palace walls

But most thro' midnight streets I hear
How the youthful Harlots curse
Blasts the new-born Infants tear
And blights with plagues the Marriage hearse

questions.prompt: What are 'mind-forg'd manacles'?
Match each image to the institution Blake criticises.
Explain the play on the word 'mark' in lines 3–4.
questions.memo:
✓ First 'mark' means to notice (1)
✓ 'Marks' means visible signs/scars of suffering on people's faces (1)

sections.title: QUESTION 5: The Novel: Theme, Symbol and Narrative Technique
sections.instructions: Read the text below, then answer the questions.

context.title: Practice extract (written for FreeSheet)
context.text:
The jacaranda had been planted the year my father was born, and for as long as I could remember it had flowered every October, carpeting the driveway in purple. My father used to complain about the mess. 'One day I'll cut that thing down,' he would say, sweeping, though we all knew he never would.

The October after he died, the tree did not flower. My mother said it was the drought. My brother said it was coincidence. I said nothing, but I stood under its bare branches every afternoon, waiting, as if it owed me something.

It was only later, much later, that I understood why I had been so angry with a tree.

questions.prompt: Which is a statement of THEME rather than subject?
options: Grief can make us look for meaning in ordinary things

questions.prompt: What is a hint about future events in a story called?
A motif is a recurring image or idea in a text.
The practice extract is narrated in the…
Explain the irony of the father's words 'One day I'll cut that thing down'.
questions.memo:
✓ He complained about the tree but never cut it down; he secretly loved it (1)
✓ After his death, the tree 'dies' in a sense on its own (1)

questions.prompt: What is the effect of the final sentence?
questions.memo:
✓ It shows the narrator is looking back with greater understanding (retrospective narration) (1)
✓ and suggests the anger was really grief for the father, inviting reflection (1)

sections.title: QUESTION 7: Visual Literacy: Advertisements, Cartoons and Film
sections.instructions: Read the text below, then answer the questions.

context.title: Described film still (original)
context.text: A low-angle shot shows a factory owner standing on a balcony, silhouetted against a red evening sky. Below him, in a high-angle long shot, workers queue at the factory gates. A slow, heavy drumbeat plays on the soundtrack.

questions.prompt: A low-angle shot usually makes a character appear…
Which type of shot best shows a character's emotion in detail?
Pathos is an appeal to the audience's emotions.
Discuss how camera angles in the described film still show the relationship between the owner and the workers.
questions.memo:
✓ The low angle makes the owner look powerful/dominant (1)
✓ The high-angle long shot makes the workers look small, powerless and numerous (1)
✓ The contrast emphasises inequality/a power imbalance (1)

questions.prompt: Why might the director show the owner as a silhouette?
questions.memo:
✓ It hides his face, making him seem mysterious/impersonal (1)
✓ suggesting he is distant from or uncaring towards the workers (1)
